subtype: Approach: mass applying with one generic resume [Pitfall]
passage:
By the third week Sarita had sent 240 applications, all with the same resume, and her spreadsheet was a wall of grey Applied cells. Each evening the portal buzzed with new job alerts, and each night she clicked Apply twenty times, feeling like a machine of productivity. Replies: two automatic rejections, nothing else. “The market is dead,” she told her roommate Joseph, who was making tea.
“Maybe,” Joseph said. “What does the resume say about backend jobs?”
“It says... everything.”
“Then how would they know what it's for?”
Sarita shrugged and opened the portal again. It was easier to click than to rewrite.

qa.q: How many applications had Sarita sent?
What might Sarita feel when she says the market is dead?
qa.a: Sarita may feel frustrated and defensive, blaming the market to avoid the harder thought that the resume is not working.
Sarita could tailor the resume to the skills each role lists and send fewer, better applications, since a clear signal of fit gets replies.

qa.q: How might Joseph see Sarita's clicking?
qa.a: Joseph sees a vague resume and asks a gentle question, probably concerned but unable to force a change.

grounding: Sending the same resume to hundreds of portals feels productive, but replies stay near zero, and the student blames the market instead of the resume.

subtype: Approach: mass applying with one generic resume [Pitfall]
passage:
"Two hundred and twelve applications, Aparna. Two hundred and twelve. Three replies. Two were rejections."
"Which resume did you send?"
"The resume. My resume."
"The same one? To all of them?"
"It's a good resume! Marks, projects, everything."
"Yash, which projects are on it?"
"The college library app, the line-follower robot, the chat bot."
"And what were the jobs?"
"Everything. Data analyst, testing, support, frontend, one sales role."
"So a data company reads about a robot, and a sales company reads about a library app."
"..."
"Nothing on it tells them why you fit them."
"The market is just dead right now. Everyone says so."
"Maybe it's slow. But people from our class got calls. Pick five jobs you actually want. Change the top of the resume for each one."
"Five? That feels like nothing."
"Two hundred felt like something. Did it work?"

qa.q: How many applications had Yash sent?
qa.a: Yash had sent two hundred and twelve.

qa.q: How does Yash feel about the three replies?
qa.a: Yash is frustrated and defensive, blaming a dead market rather than the resume.

qa.q: What would you change first in Yash's search?
qa.a: Pick a few roles that truly fit and adjust the top of the resume for each, so every application shows why Yash suits that job.

qa.q: How does Aparna see the two hundred applications?
qa.a: Aparna sees them as busy but aimless, since one resume sent everywhere tells no company why Yash fits them.

grounding: Shows a student sending one generic resume to hundreds of openings, getting almost no replies, and blaming the market instead of the resume.

subtype: Approach: mass applying with one generic resume [Pitfall]
passage: In my final semester, I treated job portals like a lottery. I'm Mehak. Every night I'd open five sites and click "easy apply" on anything with "fresher" in the title. Same resume, same one-line note. By March I'd sent over three hundred. Replies: almost none. I told everyone the market was terrible, and honestly, I believed it. I even told my mother that companies weren't hiring freshers from colleges like mine. Then Salma, my hostel roommate, asked to see the resume. She read it twice and said, gently, "Mehak, this could be anyone's." She was right. Nothing on it said hire me for this job. Looking back, sending three hundred felt productive every single night. It was just a very tiring way of saying nothing.

qa.q: How many applications had Mehak sent by March?
qa.a: Mehak had sent over three hundred.

qa.q: How did Mehak feel about the lack of replies at the time?
qa.a: Mehak felt discouraged and bitter about the market, truly believing companies weren't hiring freshers.

qa.q: What else could Mehak have tried instead of easy apply?
qa.a: Mehak could have chosen fewer roles and tailored the resume and note to each, or asked a placement officer to review them.

qa.q: How does Salma see Mehak's resume?
qa.a: Salma sees that it could belong to anyone and says so gently, pointing to the real problem Mehak had missed.

grounding: Illustrates a student mass-applying with one generic resume, getting almost no replies, and blaming the market until a friend points to the resume.
